## Learning Objectives 

This section covers the following topics:

- Creation of `sf::LINESTRING` and `sf::MULTIPOLYGON` objects from raw data.  

- Loading map polygons from `map_data()`  

- Building buffers, unions, and hulls around sampling locations.  

- Measuring land cover inside polygons.  

- Importing data from ESRI shapefile.  

- Implementing Spatial Joins.





# Lines {background-color="black" background-image="media/contour.png" background-size="initial" background-position="right"}

```{r startup, include=FALSE}
library(sf)
library(ggplot2)
library(tidyverse)
library(fontawesome)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  fig.retina = 3,
  warning = FALSE,
  message = FALSE,
  fig.align = "center"
)
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 20))
```



## Data Sources: *De novo* Creation {.scrollable .smaller}

It is possible to make data from scratch by entering coordinates directly.


```{r}
set.seed(543)
df <- data.frame(
  id = c(rep("Rodney", 5), rep("Sarah", 5)),
  Data = rnorm(10, 42, 42),
  Longitude = rnorm(10, -78, 1),
  Latitude = rnorm(10, 37, 1)
)
df
```

## Data Sources: *De novo* Creation  {.scrollable .smaller}

To make them into `sf` `POINT` objects, use `st_as_sf()` as normal.

```{r}
df |>
  st_as_sf(coords = c("Longitude", "Latitude"), crs = 4326) -> pts
pts
```


## Plotting Points {.smaller}

We can easily mix individual aesthetic properties to change the representation of the points provided by using `geom_sf()`.


```{r eval=FALSE}
ggplot(pts) +
  geom_sf(aes(color = id, size = Data)) +
  coord_sf() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, vjust = 1, hjust = 1))
```



```{r}
#| echo: false
ggplot(pts) +
  geom_sf(aes(color = id, size = Data)) +
  coord_sf() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, vjust = 1, hjust = 1))
```






## Data Sources: *De novo* Creation

To make `sf` as `LINESTRING` we can group by the id value and then we need to summarize the `Data` component, then cast it to a Linestring.

```{r}
df |>
  st_as_sf(coords = c("Longitude", "Latitude"), crs = 4326) |>
  group_by(id) |>
  summarize(Data = mean(Data)) |>
  st_cast("LINESTRING") -> lines
```

## &nbsp; {.scrollable}

```{r}
lines
```

## Operations on `LINESTRING` Objects

Physical length of the `LINESTRING` objects.  

```{r}
st_length(lines)
```


## Operations on `LINESTRING` Objects


The bounding box around all the lines.

```{r}
st_bbox(lines)
```

## Operations on `LINESTRING` Objects

The area of the convex hull encompassing *all* the lines.
```{r}
library(units)
lines |>
  st_union() |>
  st_convex_hull() |>
  st_area() |>
  set_units(km^2)
```


## Textual Versions of `geometry`

Any geometry can be written out as *Well Known Text* (WKT), a plain-text description of its shape and coordinates.


```{r}
lines$geometry[1] |> st_as_text()
```




# Polygons {background-color="black" background-image="media/contour.png" background-size="initial" background-position="right"}

`r fa("circle-notch", fill='limegreen')`



## Polygons

Polygons are simply lines whose first and last coordinate are exactly the same.

:::{.fragment}

```{r}
df.p <- df[c(1:5, 1, 6:10, 6), ]
df.p
```
:::

## Polygon *de novo* Creation

Use `st_cast()` as before to make groups of points into a polygon.

:::{.fragment}

```{r}
df |>
  st_as_sf(coords = c("Longitude", "Latitude"), crs = 4326) |>
  group_by(id) |>
  summarize(Data = mean(Data)) |>
  st_cast("POLYGON") -> polygons
```

:::


## &nbsp;

```{r}
polygons
```


## Visualizing Polygon Objects {.smaller}

```{r}
ggplot(polygons) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = Data), alpha = 0.75) +
  coord_sf() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, vjust = 0.5, hjust = 1))
```

## Polygons From Data Frames

The `ggplot` library provides access to map data as well.

```{r}
map_data("county", "virginia") |>
  select(
    Longitude = long,
    Latitude = lat,
    group,
    County = subregion
  ) -> va_counties
```

## Polygons From Data Frames

```{r}
head(va_counties)
```


## 

```{r fig.width=12}
ggplot(va_counties, aes(Longitude, Latitude)) +
  geom_point(size = 0.25) +
  coord_quickmap() # roughly spherical projection
```


##

```{r}
va_counties |>
  filter(County %in% c("hanover", "henrico")) |>
  ggplot(aes(Longitude, Latitude)) +
  geom_polygon(aes(fill = County), alpha = 0.1) +
  geom_point(aes(color = County)) +
  coord_quickmap()
```

##

```{r fig.width=10}
ggplot(va_counties, aes(Longitude, Latitude)) +
  geom_polygon(
    aes(group = group),
    fill = "grey80",
    color = "black",
    linewidth = 0.25
  ) +
  coord_quickmap()
```


## Combining polygons and `sf` objects

```{r}
ggplot() +
  geom_polygon(
    aes(Longitude, Latitude, group = group),
    fill = "grey80",
    color = "black",
    linewidth = 0.25,
    data = va_counties
  ) +
  geom_sf(aes(color = Data), lwd = 3, data = lines) +
  coord_sf()
```





# Buffers & Neighborhoods {background-color="black" background-image="media/contour.png" background-size="initial" background-position="right"}


## Dogwood Trees

Maternal dogwood trees sampled from the city of Richmond south to Pocahontas State Park.  We start with the 15 `Preliminary` trees (5 per `Habitat`), sorted south to north.

```{r}
dogwood_url <- "https://dyerlabteaching.github.io/CourseData/Spatial/Richmond_Dogwoods.csv"
read_csv(dogwood_url) |>
  filter(Preliminary) |>
  select(-Preliminary) |>
  arrange(Latitude, Longitude) |>
  st_as_sf(coords = c("Longitude", "Latitude"), crs = 4326) |>
  st_transform(crs = 32617) -> trees
```

:::{.fragment}
<font color="red">Buffers & areas use the CRS units: reproject to meters (UTM 17N) first!</font>
:::


## &nbsp; {.scrollable}

```{r}
trees
```


## Plot the Trees

```{r}
ggplot(trees) + geom_sf(aes(color = Habitat), size = 4) + coord_sf()
```


## Buffers

Everything within some distance of a feature.  Buffering a `POINT` makes a `POLYGON`.

```{r}
trees |>
  st_buffer(dist = 250) -> nbhd
st_area(nbhd) |> head(n = 3)
```

:::{.fragment}
Compare to $\pi r^2$

```{r}
pi * 250^2
```
:::


## Unions

`summarize()` on an `sf` object unions the geometries in each group.

```{r}
nbhd |>
  group_by(Habitat) |>
  summarize() -> habitat_nbhd
habitat_nbhd |>
  st_area() |>
  set_units(km^2)
```

:::{.fragment}
Five buffers would be `r round( 5 * pi * 250^2 / 1e6, 2 )` km²; overlaps are only counted once.
:::


## Convex Hulls

The smallest convex polygon around a set of points (a rubber band).

```{r}
trees |>
  group_by(Habitat) |>
  summarize() |>
  st_convex_hull() -> hulls
st_area(hulls) |> set_units(km^2)
```


## A Transect Corridor

Trees are sorted south to north, so the ends are the first and last rows (the function `slice()` allows us to pull specific rows based on index).

```{r}
trees |>
  slice(c(1, n())) |>
  summarize() |>
  st_cast("LINESTRING") -> transect
```


## A Transect Corridor

How long is the transect?

```{r}
st_length(transect) |>
  set_units(km)
```

## A Transect Coorridor

Let's visualize it by adding a quick buffer around it.

```{r}
transect |> st_buffer(dist = 250) -> corridor
```

## &nbsp;

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 10
ggplot() +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = Habitat), alpha = 0.2, data = hulls) +
  geom_sf(fill = "grey60", color = NA, data = corridor) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = Habitat), data = nbhd) +
  geom_sf(data = trees, size = 0.5) +
  coord_sf() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
```

# Land Cover {background-color="black" background-image="media/contour.png" background-size="initial" background-position="right"}


## National Land Cover Database

<a href="https://www.mrlc.gov/data" target="_blank">NLCD</a>: every 30 m × 30 m cell of the US classified into land cover (water, developed, forest, wetlands, agriculture, ...).

:::{.fragment}
This is a *raster*, which we cover later.  For now, it is a black box:

```{r}
source("https://dyerlabteaching.github.io/Vector-Data/get_landcover.R")
```

`get_landcover( polygons )` $\to$ proportion of each polygon in 7 categories.
:::


## Land Cover in Each Neighborhood {.scrollable}

```{r}
lc <- get_landcover(nbhd)
lc
```


## Summarize by Habitat {.smaller .scrollable}

```{r}
lc |>
  group_by(Habitat, Category) |>
  summarize(Proportion = mean(Proportion), .groups = "drop") -> habitat_lc
```

:::{.fragment}
**Why `.groups = "drop"`?**  

`summarize()` only peels off the *last* grouping variable (`Category`), so without it the result is still grouped by `Habitat`, and `dplyr` prints a message telling you so.

:::{.fragment}
```{r}
#| message: true
lc |>
  group_by(Habitat, Category) |>
  summarize(Proportion = mean(Proportion)) |>
  group_vars()
```

We reuse `habitat_lc` for a table, a plot, and a comparison with the transect.  A leftover grouping would quietly change how any later `mutate()` or `summarize()` works on it.  `.groups = "drop"` hands back a plain, ungrouped table.
:::
:::


## Pivoting the Data

We have the normal `tidy` output of data.

```{r}
head(habitat_lc)
```

:::{.fragment}

But would like to make a table that has columns of Categores and rows of habitat.  We have to `pivot` the data frame from **long** to **wide**.

```{r}
#| eval: false 
?pivot_wider
```
:::

## Summarize by Habitat

```{r}
habitat_lc |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = Habitat, values_from = Proportion) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```



## &nbsp;

```{r}
#| fig-width: 10
ggplot(habitat_lc, aes(Category, Proportion, fill = Habitat)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Average proportion of a 250 m neighborhood")
```

# Shapefiles 🤷  {background-color="black" background-image="media/contour.png" background-size="initial" background-position="right"}


## &nbsp; {background-color="white" background-image="https://dyerlabteaching.github.io/Vector-Data/media/shapefile_definition_chatGPT3.png" background-size="contain" background-position="center"}



## Shapefiles

The ESRI *Shapefile* is a non-standardized format for packaging vector based data (`POINT`, `LINESTRING`, `POLYGON`, etc.).  

However, it is not actually a file but it is a collection of files, which may (or may not) expand directly in the folder or within a subfolder.


![](media/flickr_50540213032.jpg){fig-alt="A file listing showing Zoning_Districts.cpg, .dbf, .prj, .shp, and .shx files, and a folder named Centerlines-shp."}


## Archived ZIP Files.

I've put some shapefiles in the [course data repository](https://dyerlabteaching.github.io/CourseData/).  These are from the Richmond City GIS Department and represent the centerlines of roads in the city as well as the zoning districts.

Here are the URL's for both of these files.

```{r}
roads_url <- "https://dyerlabteaching.github.io/CourseData/Spatial/Richmond_Roads.zip"
district_url <- "https://dyerlabteaching.github.io/CourseData/Spatial/Richmond_ZoningDistricts.zip"
```


## Downloading Files Using R

You can use your browser and copy and paste those addresses in to download the files to your computer.  Then you'll have to move those archives to your PROJECT FOLDER (you are using Projects right?).

:::{.fragment}

`OR`

You can have `R` download the file and save it locally.

```{r}
shp_dir <- tempdir() # on your computer, use your project's data folder
download.file(district_url, destfile = file.path(shp_dir, "Districts.zip"))
download.file(roads_url, destfile = file.path(shp_dir, "Roads.zip"))
```

:::

## Unzipping Files

You can open your computer finder and have the OS unzip the archives.

`OR`

You can have `R` do it.

```{r}
unzip(file.path(shp_dir, "Districts.zip"), exdir = shp_dir)
unzip(file.path(shp_dir, "Roads.zip"), exdir = shp_dir)
```



## File Components


![](media/flickr_54843115636.jpg){fig-alt="A project folder listing showing Districts.zip and Roads.zip, the unzipped Centerlines-shp folder, and the five Zoning_Districts component files (.cpg, .dbf, .prj, .shp, .shx) with their sizes."}


## The Projection File

![](media/flickr_50540256782.jpg){fig-alt="The Zoning_Districts.prj file open in RStudio, showing the well-known-text definition of NAD83 Virginia South (US feet): a Lambert Conformal Conic projection on the GRS 1980 spheroid."}

## Loading A Shapefile

You can load it in using `sf::st_read()` and passing it the `.shp` file path to it.

```{r}
st_read(file.path(shp_dir, "Zoning_Districts.shp")) -> districts
```

## Shapefiles Convert to `sf` Objects {.smaller .scrollable}

By default, the data associated with a vector object are put into a `data.frame` and the `geometry` object is properly created.

```{r}
head(districts, n = 2)
```

## Simplifying Data

```{r}
names(districts)
```

## Simplifying Data

```{r}
districts |>
  dplyr::select(-Comment, -CreatedBy, -CreatedDat, -EditBy, -EditDate) |>
  dplyr::select(-Shape__Are, -Shape__Len) -> districts
head(districts, n = 1)
```


## District Codes

```{r}
districts$Name |> unique() |> sort()
```



## Visualizing 

```{r}
plot(districts["Name"])
```


## Visualizing Overlays


```{r}
plot(st_geometry(districts))
plot(
  st_geometry(districts[districts$OBJECTID == 530, ]),
  col = 'red',
  add = TRUE
)
```




# Vector Operations  {background-color="black" background-image="media/contour.png" background-size="initial" background-position="right"}


## Spatial Joins

We can combine spatial data sets by *where* their features are (intersect, touch, contain, within some distance) instead of by a shared column.  These are `spatial joins`.

There are a wide variety of operations available:

<center><font color="red">Check out the [Cheatsheet](https://github.com/rstudio/cheatsheets/blob/main/sf.pdf)</font></center>




## Secondary Vector Data Set

```{r}
road.shapefile <- st_read(file.path(
  shp_dir,
  "Centerlines-shp/tran_Carriageway.shp"
))
```

## Secondary Vector Data Set

```{r}
names(road.shapefile)
```


## Check Projections

<font color="red">Dyer's First Rule: Make Sure Projections Are the Same</font>


```{r}
st_crs(road.shapefile) == st_crs(districts)
```

:::{.fragment}
If they differed, one could do something like:

```{r eval=FALSE}
road.shapefile |>
  st_transform(crs = st_crs(districts)) -> road.shapefile
```
:::








## Data Cleanup {.scrollable .smaller}

```{r}
road.shapefile |>
  select(
    FullName,
    OneWay,
    StreetType,
    SpeedLimit = PostedSpee,
    Length = SHAPE_Leng,
    geometry
  ) |>
  mutate(OneWay = factor(OneWay), StreetType = factor(StreetType)) -> roads
summary(roads)
```



## Visualizing: Filter Highways & Plot
```{r}
roads |>
  filter(
    StreetType %in% c("Highway", "Highway Interchange", "Ramp")
  ) -> highways
summary(highways)
```


## Plot It 

Let's color this based upon SpeedLimit

```{r echo=FALSE}
plot(highways["SpeedLimit"], lwd = 4)
```

## Intersection Plotting

Let's grab a bit of zoning from *The Fan*

```{r}
districts |>
  filter(OBJECTID == 368) |>
  st_buffer(dist = 1500) |>
  st_bbox() -> fan_bbox

districts |>
  st_crop(fan_bbox) -> theFan
```


## 

```{r}
plot(theFan["Name"])
```


## Zoning Categories {.smaller .scrollable}

`r length( unique( theFan$Name ) )` zoning codes is too many to map.  Make it a `factor` and collapse the levels with `fct_collapse()` (from [Factors](https://dyerlabteaching.github.io/Factors/slides.html)): *New Level* = *Old Levels*.

```{r}
theFan |>
  mutate(
    Name = factor(Name),
    Category = fct_collapse(
      Name,
      Residential = c(
        "R-2",
        "R-48",
        "R-5",
        "R-53",
        "R-6",
        "R-63",
        "R-7",
        "R-73"
      ),
      `Residential Office` = c("RO-2", "RO-3"),
      Business = c(
        "B-1",
        "B-2",
        "B-3",
        "B-4",
        "B-5",
        "B-6",
        "B-7"
      ),
      `Urban Business` = c(
        "UB",
        "UB-2",
        "UB-PO2",
        "UB-PO3",
        "UB-PO4"
      ),
      Industrial = c("M-1", "M-2"),
      Institutional = "I",
      `Transit-Oriented` = "TOD-1"
    )
  ) |>
  select(OBJECTID, Name, Category, everything()) -> theFan
```

## &nbsp;

```{r}
summary(theFan)
```


## &nbsp;

```{r fig.width=12}
ggplot(theFan) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = Category)) +
  scale_fill_brewer(type = "qual", palette = "Set3") +
  theme_void()
```



## Cropping Roads

```{r}
roads |> st_crop(st_bbox(theFan)) -> fanRoads
plot(st_geometry(fanRoads))
```


## Selecting a Single Zone


Add an attribute to the POLYGON's indicating if the district is that big one in the middle of the plot.  Let's plot it to see what the ID is.

```{r}
theFan |>
  mutate(Target = ifelse(OBJECTID == 368, TRUE, FALSE)) -> theFan
```


## Plot it
```{r}
theFan |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = Target)) +
  geom_sf_text(aes(label = OBJECTID), size = 3) +
  coord_sf() +
  theme_void()
```



## Isolate the District

```{r}
target <- theFan[theFan$OBJECTID == 368, ]
plot(st_geometry(target))
```



## &nbsp;

Keep the roads that intersect the target with `st_filter()`.

```{r}
fanRoads |>
  st_filter(target) -> targetRoads
targetRoads |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  select(`Street Name` = FullName) |>
  distinct() |>
  arrange(`Street Name`)
```


## &nbsp;

```{r}
targetRoads |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = target) +
  geom_sf(color = "darkgreen") +
  theme_void()
```



## Joining Attributes: `st_join()`

Each road segment picks up the columns of the district(s) its geometry *intersects*.

```{r}
fanRoads |>
  st_join(theFan |> select(Category)) |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  count(Category, sort = TRUE) |>
  head()
```


## Cutting Features: `st_intersection()`

Keep only the *parts* that overlap; e.g., km of road inside the target.

```{r}
fanRoads |>
  st_intersection(st_geometry(target)) |>
  st_length() |>
  sum() |>
  set_units(km)
```
